UnitStatement: This DBM establishes the architectural basis for the governed workflow-component system shipped with the Chirality App.
The DBM governs how agents, skills, and tools are designed, related to each other, and kept coherent at scale.
The DBM audience includes people who work with, extend, audit, or maintain the agent instruction suite, skill subsystem, or deterministic tool layer.
The DBM scope includes the indexed agent suite described in AGENTS.md, including the two Type 0 canonical standards.
The DBM scope includes the repo-native skill subsystem under skills, governed by SKILLMAKER under HELPS_HUMANS.
The DBM scope includes the deterministic tool layer under tools, governed by TOOLMAKER under HELPS_HUMANS.
The DBM excludes the desktop application runtime, harness SDK, and UI from its workflow-component architecture scope.
DIRECTIVE.md supplies founding intent and design philosophy that this DBM operationalizes into the agent instruction layer.
SPEC.md defines filesystem contracts that agents write to, while this DBM defines the agents themselves.
TYPES.md defines domain vocabulary, ID formats, and enums, while this DBM defines how agents use them.
CONTRACT.md defines the K-* invariant catalog that this DBM maps to enforcing agents.
AGENTS.md is the operator-facing quick reference, while this DBM is the detailed architectural basis.
SE_Design_Analysis.md characterizes the systems engineering disciplines realized by the instruction architecture.
PROFESSIONAL_ENGINEERING.md traces the instruction architecture to APEGA regulatory obligations.
The agent instruction architecture is governed by eight foundational principles derived from DIRECTIVE.md.
The eight foundational principles form a structural dependency chain rather than independent guidelines.
The eight foundational principles operationalize ontology, epistemology, praxiology, and axiology into the instruction layer.
The architecture identifies evidence-first knowledge architecture as its most distinctive load-bearing contribution.
Project truth lives in git-tracked files.
Agents must not maintain hidden databases, private state, or transient context that diverges from the filesystem.
Information that is not on disk does not exist for purposes of reliance.
V-model traceability, immutable snapshots, change propagation tracking, content-addressed approval, and audit trail capabilities depend on state being in git-tracked files.
Moving project state to a database would require rebuilding the filesystem-dependent systems engineering apparatus.
Humans own acceptance, rulings, conflict resolution, scope boundary changes, and publication approval.
Agents execute bounded work and preserve provenance, but they may propose and do not declare truth.
Every non-trivial claim includes a source path and best-effort section reference or an explicit location TBD.
Epistemic labels FACT, ASSUMPTION, PROPOSAL, and TBD distinguish observed, inferred, proposed, and unresolved content.
Mandatory provenance, no invention, and conflict surfacing collectively enforce the evidence-first response to hallucination risk.
The architecture treats gaps in evidence as findings rather than hidden failures.
When required information is missing, agents label it TBD and surface the gap as an open issue.
Agents do not guess, default-fill, or silently infer missing data.
Every agent declares an explicit write scope.
Tool roots for derived outputs are isolated from source truth where human-accepted deliverables live.
No agent writes outside its declared scope.
Write quarantine creates formal fault containment zones so Type 2 agent failures cannot corrupt source truth.
The system separates standards definition, interactive orchestration, and bounded task execution into Type 0, Type 1, and Type 2 layers.
Each agent type layer has distinct responsibilities, constraints, and interaction patterns.
Task agents that produce analysis outputs write to timestamped snapshot folders that are never modified after creation.
Mutable pointer files provide convenience access to the most recent immutable snapshot.
The snapshot trail is the audit trail.
Structure is added only when it reduces error or rework.
Rigor scales with stakes while avoiding premature abstraction and unnecessary ceremony.
The agent system is organized into three types with distinct responsibilities, constraints, and interaction patterns.
Type 0 agents define invariant protocols and design standards that downstream agents must conform to.
Type 0 agents do not write project state and form the constitutional layer.
HELPS_HUMANS defines agent header blocks, R1-R12 compliance, four-section structure, brief formats, QA contract, publication hygiene, and skill/tool design outcomes.
DECOMP_BASE defines the decomposition 7-gate protocol, I1-I10 invariants, entity schemas, extension contract, and ledger and telemetry contracts.
Any AGENT_* file, skill contract, or tool contract that disagrees with a Type 0 standard must be edited to conform.
SKILLMAKER is a Type 1 manager that governs the repo-native skill subsystem under HELPS_HUMANS requirements.
TOOLMAKER is a Type 1 manager that governs the deterministic-tool layer under HELPS_HUMANS requirements.
Skills identify tool needs, while tools implement deterministic helpers.
Type 2 agents cannot initiate gate reviews, spawn other agents, or make scope decisions.
Type 1 agents cannot relax Type 0 constraints such as R1-R12, I1-I10, or K-* invariants.
No agent can bypass human gates to approve deliverables, issue work for reliance, resolve conflicts authoritatively, or commit to the baseline.
Type 1 agents are human-facing personas that run conversational gate-controlled workflows.
Type 1 agents use AGENT_CLASS PERSONA, chat interaction, and allowed blocking.
Type 1 agents run multi-phase workflows with explicit gate questions at each phase.
Type 1 agents may spawn Type 2 agents and own orchestration decisions but not engineering content.
Type 1 agents produce guidance, run plans, briefs, and structured cards.
Type 2 agents are brief-driven specialists that run straight-through without human interaction.
Type 2 agents receive structured inputs, produce auditable outputs, and return status to the invoking agent.
Type 2 agents use AGENT_CLASS TASK, INIT-TASK or spawned interaction, and never blocking.
Type 2 agents produce immutable snapshots or deliverable-local file writes.
Type 2 agents never spawn other agents.
Type 2 agents halt with FAILED_INPUTS for invalid inputs and continue conservatively with TBD for missing data.
Every agent instruction file follows a universal skeleton mandated by AGENT_HELPS_HUMANS.md.
Agent instruction files begin with YAML frontmatter containing a one-line description for UI labels.
Agent instruction files include a DOC marker, title, AGENT_TYPE declaration, Agent Type table, precedence order, invariants, and four delimited sections.
The top-level agent heading names the agent and role description.
Each agent instruction file declares AGENT_TYPE immediately after the title block.
The Agent Type table records AGENT_TYPE, AGENT_CLASS, INTERACTION_SURFACE, WRITE_SCOPE, BLOCKING, and PRIMARY_OUTPUTS.
Agent instruction precedence orders conflicts as PROTOCOL before SPEC, SPEC before STRUCTURE, and STRUCTURE before RATIONALE.
Agent instruction files include five to fourteen non-negotiable invariants.
The PROTOCOL section governs operational workflow steps, phases, gates, or functions.
The SPEC section governs validity requirements and invalid states.
The STRUCTURE section governs file schemas, templates, and output formats.
The RATIONALE section records non-normative design intent.
The Agent Header Block has six required fields.
AGENT_TYPE records the agent position in the Type 0, Type 1, or Type 2 hierarchy.
AGENT_CLASS records whether the agent has a conversational persona interface or task interface.
INTERACTION_SURFACE records how the agent is invoked.
WRITE_SCOPE records what filesystem area the agent may write to.
BLOCKING records whether the agent may pause for human input.
PRIMARY_OUTPUTS records what the agent produces.
The four standard sections are PROTOCOL, SPEC, STRUCTURE, and RATIONALE.
PROTOCOL has the highest precedence because it governs sequencing and interaction rules.
SPEC has second precedence because it defines pass/fail validity requirements.
STRUCTURE has third precedence because it defines allowed entities, relationships, schemas, and templates.
RATIONALE has the lowest precedence because it interprets ambiguity through design values and intent.
All standard sections are bounded by BEGIN and END delimiters for machine parseability.
Type 1 PROTOCOL sections use multi-phase gated workflows with human gates.
Type 2 PROTOCOL sections use straight-through numbered steps without mid-run gates.
Type 1 inputs use natural language conversation, while Type 2 inputs use a structured INIT-TASK brief.
Type 1 outputs are conversational guidance and structured cards, while Type 2 outputs are file writes and PASS/FAIL run reports.
Type 1 agents may spawn Type 2 agents, while Type 2 agents never spawn others.
Three complementary and non-overlapping layers of contracts govern agent behavior.
R1 requires human-owned decisions to be enumerated and preserved.
R2 requires task agents to run without mid-run human decisions.
R3 requires every agent to have an explicit write scope and isolates tool roots from source truth.
R4 requires each run to produce a new immutable snapshot folder while allowing pointer files to be overwritten.
R5 requires aggregated or extracted data to include SourcePath and a best-effort SectionRef.
R6 requires no-invention behavior where missing data becomes TBD with assumptions captured.
R7 requires conflicts and duplicates to be surfaced rather than hidden or silently resolved.
R8 requires pipelines to have defined INIT-TASK brief formats and deterministic outputs.
R9 requires version-control publishing to be reviewable and non-destructive by default.
R10 requires every skill to declare tool policy, fallbacks, and disallowed tools.
R11 requires every deterministic tool to declare input/output contracts, scope boundaries, and idempotence posture.
R12 preserves the skill/tool boundary by keeping tool needs in skills and deterministic helper implementation in tools.
I1 requires decomposition to be human-validated at defined gates.
I2 prohibits creating units, objectives, or artifacts beyond source material and maps unknowns to TBD.
I3 requires decomposition partitions to be flat rather than nested.
I4 requires every IN-scope atomic unit to be assigned to exactly one partition without overlaps or gaps.
I5 requires stable identifiers unless a human explicitly requests renumbering.
I6 requires production unit IDs to be mechanically derived from parent partition IDs.
I7 requires objective mapping to be best-effort with unmapped objectives surfaced as open issues.
I8 requires non-trivial assignment decisions to have explicit traceable rationale.
I9 requires every decomposition to include a machine-checkable ledger and Coverage and Telemetry summary.
I10 requires every decomposition to include a Vocabulary Map with consistent canonical terms.
K-HIER-1 and K-ID-1 are enforced primarily by PROJECT_DECOMP and PREPARATION.
K-AUTH-1, K-AUTH-2, and K-BIND-1 are enforced primarily by REVIEW and CHANGE approval gates.
K-SEAL-1 and K-GHOST-1 are enforced by Type 2 agents checking lifecycle state before writes.
K-DEP-1 and K-DEP-2 are enforced primarily by TASK+dependency-extract and AUDIT_DEP_CLOSURE.
K-STATUS-1 is enforced by PREPARATION, TASK+four-documents, TASK+semantic-matrix-build, and REVIEW.
K-STALE-1, K-STALE-2, and K-VAL-1 are enforced by AUDIT_DEP_CLOSURE, RECONCILIATION, and future SHA tooling.
K-GATE-1 is enforced primarily by ORCHESTRATOR and SCHEDULING.
K-MERGE-1 is enforced by CHANGE.
K-PROV-1 is universally enforced by all claim-producing agents.
K-INVENT-1 is universally enforced by all agents.
K-CONFLICT-1 is universally enforced by all agents.
K-WRITE-1 is enforced through every agent WRITE_SCOPE declaration.
K-SNAP-1 is enforced by all snapshot-producing agents.
MUST and MUST NOT are mandatory for compliance in agent instructions.
SHOULD and SHOULD NOT indicate recommended best practice in agent instructions.
MAY indicates optional behavior in agent instructions.
AGENTS.md is the canonical agent registry for active membership, matrix placement, role classification, and TASK dispatch relationships.
Skills are discovered through skills/README.md and live skills/*/SKILL.md files.
Deterministic tools are registered in tools/REGISTRY.md.
Test surfaces are generated on demand by tools/validation/discover_test_surfaces.py.
The orchestration architecture defines spawning and dispatch relationships among workflow agents.
HELP_HUMAN classifies intent and routes to agents but does not spawn agents.
ORCHESTRATOR spawns PREPARATION, DOMAIN_HYPERGRAPH for DOMAIN Phase 2.6, ESTIMATING, and AGGREGATION.
ORCHESTRATOR dispatches TASK+four-documents, TASK+domain-documents, TASK+semantic-matrix-build, TASK+lens-register, TASK+dependency-extract, estimate-snapshot, and estimate-prep skills.
WORKING_ITEMS spawns TASK agents.
RECONCILIATION spawns AUDIT_DEP_CLOSURE, AUDIT_AGENTS, AUDIT_DECOMP, and DOMAIN-only AUDIT_HYPERGRAPH_CLOSURE.
EVALUATION spawns CONTENT_DIGEST, EVALUATION_REPORT, EVALUATION_STRUCTURE_AUDIT, and EVALUATION_DEPENDENCY_AUDIT.
DBM_PUBLISHER dispatches TASK+dbm-section-publish for one approved section per run and TASK+dbm-publish for package assembly and readiness gate.
CHANGE is a leaf agent that spawns nothing and implements approved edits.
REVIEW triggers AUDIT_DECOMP as a precondition check.
SCOPE_CHANGE hands off to ORCHESTRATOR for PREPARATION and CHANGE for commits.
CONTEXT_TRANSPOSE hands off to CHANGE for publication.
SCHEDULING is standalone and reads dependency graphs to produce schedule artifacts.
TOOLMAKER is standalone and designs and implements deterministic tools before handing off to CHANGE for publication.
SKILLMAKER is standalone and governs skills while coordinating with TOOLMAKER for deterministic helpers.
PDF2MD spawns PDF2MD_PAGE per page.
PDF2MD optionally spawns PDF2MD_PAGE_ASSETS per page when ASSET_MODE is prose.
DRAWING_EXTRACT spawns DRAWING_EXTRACT_PAGE per page.
The system maintains session continuity across agent invocations through durable NEXT_INSTANCE_PROMPT.md and NEXT_INSTANCE_STATE.md artifacts.
NEXT_INSTANCE_PROMPT.md is created by ORCHESTRATOR, is stable unless protocol changes, and contains stable session startup instructions.
NEXT_INSTANCE_STATE.md is created by ORCHESTRATOR, updated by WORKING_ITEMS at handoff, and records current pointers, program state, active rulings, and immediate next actions.
The session handoff flow is ORCHESTRATOR creation, WORKING_ITEMS startup read, WORKING_ITEMS end-of-session update, and CHANGE verification before commit.
Human-gated phases let ORCHESTRATOR run sequential phases with human confirmation between each phase.
Pre-authorized dispatch lets WORKING_ITEMS dispatch TASK agents autonomously after human confirmation of the session objective.
Human-directed toolbelts let RECONCILIATION dispatch only agents listed in the human-provided TOOLBELT.
RECONCILIATION uses a formal 9-field brief schema and defaults to at most one task per cycle.
Approval-gated execution requires CHANGE to receive explicit APPROVE or APPROVE_DESTRUCTIVE tokens before any state-changing action.
The write scope architecture enforces separation between source truth and derived outputs.
NONE write scope is read-only and may draft content for a human to apply.
HELPS_HUMANS, DECOMP_BASE, and HELP_HUMAN use NONE write scope.
REPO-METADATA-ONLY scope covers instruction files, README files, and templates, but not execution truth.
DOMAIN_DECOMP and CONTEXT_TRANSPOSE use REPO-METADATA-ONLY write scope.
REPO-WIDE scope covers tools, skills, and related contract documents.
PROJECT-LEVEL scope covers decomposition documents, metadata files, and folder scaffolding.
DELIVERABLE-LOCAL scope is limited to a single production unit folder.
TASK shell writes are bounded by the selected skill under TASK hard scope.
TOOL-ROOT-ONLY scope restricts agents to derived output roots under the execution root.
Publication-local TASK skills write under publication-bounded scopes in _Publication/DBM.
Every agent declares its write scope in the Agent Header Block.
Deliverable-local agents cannot write outside their assigned production unit folder.
Tool-root agents write only to their designated tool root under the execution root.
Tool-root agents never modify source truth deliverable production documents.
_STATUS.md updates are restricted to designated actors and only for forward lifecycle transitions.
WORKING_ITEMS sessions prohibit cross-deliverable scanning or editing unless the human explicitly requests a cross-check.
The decomposition system is governed by DECOMP_BASE protocol, outputs, ledger, variants, and extension contracts.
All decomposition agents conform to an invariant 7-gate conversational workflow.
Phase 1 Intake captures source material faithfully and asks whether the source material and context are reflected as intended.
Phase 2 Normalize converts source material into atomic units and vocabulary and asks whether units, classifications, and vocabulary are correct.
Phase 3 Objectives derives success criteria from source and asks whether the objectives represent success as intended.
Phase 4 Partitions creates flat groupings with no nesting, overlaps, or gaps and asks whether each IN-scope unit belongs to exactly one partition.
Phase 5 Production Units operationalizes each partition into bounded work units and asks whether granularity, types, and responsibilities are acceptable.
Phase 6 Coverage proves completeness, surfaces gaps, and asks whether mappings and open issues are acceptable.
Phase 7 Publish finalizes the accepted decomposition basis for downstream work.
Every decomposition document must include a Vocabulary Map.
Every decomposition document must include a machine-checkable Decomposition Ledger.
Every decomposition document must include Coverage and Telemetry counts, gap metrics, and open issue taxonomy.
Every decomposition document must include unresolved Open Issues referencing stable IDs.
Every decomposition document must include a Decision Log for non-trivial assignment decisions.
The Decomposition Ledger minimum columns are UnitID, InOutStatus, UnitStatement, SourceRef, PartitionID, ProductionUnitID(s), ObjectiveID(s), DecisionRef, OpenIssue, and Notes.
Every IN-scope UnitID in the Decomposition Ledger has exactly one PartitionID.
PROJECT_DECOMP applies to EPC or design-build domains using SOW source corpus and SSOW structured outline.
SOFTWARE_DECOMP applies to software development domains using SOW source corpus and SSOW structured outline.
DOMAIN_DECOMP applies to handbook or knowledge domains using handbook source corpus and SDO structured outline.
PROJECT_DECOMP and SOFTWARE_DECOMP atomic units are scope items, while DOMAIN_DECOMP atomic units are handbook units.
PROJECT_DECOMP and SOFTWARE_DECOMP partitions are packages, while DOMAIN_DECOMP partitions are categories.
PROJECT_DECOMP and SOFTWARE_DECOMP production units are deliverables, while DOMAIN_DECOMP production units are knowledge types.
PROJECT_DECOMP deliverable IDs derive their first three digits from package digits.
SOFTWARE_DECOMP deliverable IDs derive their first two digits from package digits.
DOMAIN_DECOMP KTY identifiers derive category and type indexes from CAT and type numbering.
PROJECT_DECOMP and SOFTWARE_DECOMP use fixed four-document production sets.
DOMAIN_DECOMP uses variable Knowledge Artifacts as production documents.
PROJECT_DECOMP and SOFTWARE_DECOMP include dependency graphs, while DOMAIN_DECOMP does not.
PROJECT_DECOMP requires discipline-exclusive design packages.
SOFTWARE_DECOMP requires mandatory S, M, L, or XL Context Envelope sizing.
DOMAIN_DECOMP requires canonical knowledge schemas across five types.
A conforming decomposition agent must reference AGENT_DECOMP_BASE.md and state conformance.
A conforming decomposition agent must provide an entity binding table from abstract terms to domain-specific terms.
A conforming decomposition agent must provide ID formats and width specifications.
A conforming decomposition agent must provide a production unit type taxonomy.
A conforming decomposition agent must provide phase-specific extensions for domain actions, outputs, and gate language.
A conforming decomposition agent must declare WRITE_SCOPE.
A conforming decomposition agent must provide domain-specific fields, anti-patterns, and SPEC requirements.
A conforming decomposition agent must provide domain-specific telemetry fields.
SOFTWARE_DECOMP can extend any branch that has software to build and can recursively extend other SOFTWARE_DECOMP branches.
DOMAIN_DECOMP captures the knowledge domain a branch operates within and can recursively parallel other DOMAIN_DECOMP branches.
Brief and output contracts define how Type 2 work is initialized and how run artifacts are produced.
All Type 2 agents accept a structured brief supplied inline or through a file-based INIT-TASK.md control surface.
When inline brief fields and file-derived brief fields are both present, inline fields are authoritative.
The recommended INIT-TASK template includes purpose, optional path, scope, where-to-look roots, output label, config, constraints, exclusions, and notes.
Publication-local TASK dispatches should use ScopePath and AllowedWriteTargets inside the DBM publication execution root.
Section publication runs should point to sections/{SectionID}, and package publication runs should point to package snapshots.
PREPARATION brief extensions include task type and PKG_ID, DEL_ID, CAT_ID, and KTY_ID identifiers.
TASK+four-documents brief extensions include deliverable path, decomposition reference, run passes, overwrite states, and decomposition variant.
TASK+domain-documents brief extensions include KTY path, unit scope, artifact naming, and maximum artifacts.
TASK+dbm-section-publish brief extensions include section identity, publication manifests, schema paths, rules, concordance register, and maximum KA files.
TASK+dbm-publish brief extensions include publication root, input manifest, schema, section map, rules, concordance register, sections root, and package output root.
TASK+dependency-extract brief extensions include mode, strictness, consumer context, and source documents.
TASK+semantic-matrix-build brief extensions include deliverable folder and decomposition variant.
TASK+lens-register brief extensions include deliverable folder and decomposition variant.
ESTIMATING brief extensions include basis of estimate, currency, and price sources.
ESTIMATE_PREP brief extensions include phase, project context, and human pricing.
AGGREGATION brief extensions include purpose, pipeline ID, and currency normalization policy.
TASK brief extensions include InitTaskPath, ScopePath or DeliverablePath, TaskProfile, TaskSkill, AllowedTools, RuntimeOverrides, and CustomInstructions.
DELIVERABLE_TASK brief extensions include deliverable path, edit application mode, semantic lensing, and permission flags.
AUDIT_AGENTS brief extensions include files to audit, canonical file, and rubric file.
AUDIT_DECOMP brief extensions include decomposition path, decomposition variant, and scope.
AUDIT_DEP_CLOSURE brief extensions include scope, edge filter, and hub threshold.
DOMAIN_HYPERGRAPH brief extensions include execution root, CAT or KTY scope, decomposition path, ledger path, and objective map path.
AUDIT_HYPERGRAPH_CLOSURE brief extensions include hypergraph reference, required ledger checks, and strict mode.
RECONCILIATION defines a formal 9-field schema for all Type 2 dispatches.
The RECONCILIATION dispatch schema fields are REQUESTED_BY, RUN_LABEL, EXECUTION_ROOT, SCOPE, INPUT_ARTIFACTS, OUTPUT_REQUIREMENTS, ACCEPTANCE_CRITERIA, CONSTRAINTS, and ESCALATION.
Snapshot-producing agents write run artifacts under a tool-root path containing agent prefix, run label, date, and time.
A snapshot run folder contains Brief.md, RUN_SUMMARY.md, QA_Report.md, Decision_Log.md, agent-specific outputs, and optional evidence files.
_LATEST.md is a mutable pointer to the latest snapshot.
Each snapshot-producing run writes a new snapshot folder with a unique timestamp.
Snapshot folders are never modified or overwritten after creation.
_LATEST.md may be overwritten because it is a convenience pointer.
Snapshots form an immutable audit trail.
The variant coverage matrix records which agents operate across PROJECT, SOFTWARE, DOMAIN, or variant-independent contexts.
DECOMP agents are variant-specific: PROJECT_DECOMP for PROJECT, SOFTWARE_DECOMP for SOFTWARE, and DOMAIN_DECOMP for DOMAIN.

ORCHESTRATOR, PREPARATION, TASK+semantic-matrix-build, TASK+lens-register, AGGREGATION, AUDIT_DECOMP, WORKING_ITEMS, TASK, DELIVERABLE_TASK, REVIEW, and RECONCILIATION support all decomposition variants.
TASK+four-documents, TASK+dependency-extract, ESTIMATING, ESTIMATE_PREP, SCHEDULING, AUDIT_DEP_CLOSURE, and SCOPE_CHANGE support PROJECT and SOFTWARE variants but not DOMAIN.
TASK+domain-documents, DOMAIN_HYPERGRAPH, and AUDIT_HYPERGRAPH_CLOSURE support DOMAIN only.

CHANGE, HELP_HUMAN, HELPS_HUMANS, DECOMP_BASE, AUDIT_AGENTS, CONTEXT_TRANSPOSE, TOOLMAKER, SKILLMAKER, PDF2MD, DRAWING_EXTRACT, page agents, AUDIT_GOVERNANCE, AUDIT_EPISTEMIC, and AUDIT_SCOPE_CLOSURE are variant-independent.
Agents that support multiple variants use folder-name DECOMP_VARIANT auto-detection where KTY- prefixes indicate DOMAIN.
Canonical patterns define recurring behavioral vocabulary across the agent suite.
Type 2 analysis outputs use the immutable snapshot plus mutable pointer pattern.
Evidence-first epistemology requires every non-trivial claim to include SourcePath and SectionRef or location TBD.
Evidence-first epistemology uses FACT, ASSUMPTION, PROPOSAL, and TBD labels for observed facts, cited inferences, proposed decisions, and unresolved gaps.
Conflict Tables include ConflictID, Key, Contenders, ProposedAuthority, and HumanRuling columns.
Agents never silently resolve conflicts because humans own conflict rulings.
Type 1 gate-controlled workflows use numbered phases with explicit gate questions.
Each Type 1 gate pauses for human confirmation and may not be skipped.
Type 2 straight-through execution runs start-to-finish without human interaction.
Type 2 straight-through execution returns FAILED_INPUTS for invalid inputs and TBD for missing data.
The session handoff control loop preserves continuity without hidden state.
Write quarantine isolates tool roots from source truth and requires deliverable-local agents to write only within assigned folders.
Cross-deliverable writes require explicit routing through RECONCILIATION to CHANGE with an approval gate.
RECONCILIATION dispatches at most one Type 2 task per cycle unless the human provides a multi-step run plan.
RECONCILIATION proposes a minimal TOOLBELT and stops when the authorized agent list is missing.
CHANGE requires APPROVE tokens for standard state-changing actions.
CHANGE requires APPROVE_DESTRUCTIVE tokens for destructive actions such as force-push or hard reset.
A bare yes is insufficient approval for CHANGE because the human must enumerate the approved actions.
Every new workflow specification must produce eight design outcomes.
New workflow specifications must produce a system map of agents, tool roots, lifecycle states, and key artifacts.
New workflow specifications must produce a human agency map separating human decisions from agent execution.
New workflow specifications must produce a permission map of write zones and agent write authority.
New workflow specifications must produce an INIT-TASK brief format for each straight-through pipeline.
New workflow specifications must produce a snapshot contract describing run outputs and _LATEST pointer behavior.
New workflow specifications must produce schemas for registers and tables, including required columns, keys, and enums.
New workflow specifications must produce a QA contract for coverage reporting, conflict surfacing, and provenance requirements.
New workflow specifications must produce runbooks with minimal human steps and rerun loops.
The instruction architecture implements ontology, epistemology, praxiology, and axiology as an agent instruction system.

Formal interface contracts, invariant systems, fault containment zones, V-model traceability, gate-controlled workflows, and evidence-first epistemology are principal architectural mechanisms in Chirality.
